Nat Habit · Category Research · Face Scrub New Range

The case in one line: Nat Habit already has the trust and the satisfaction — it's the format and the promise that are holding it back.

90.0% of surveyed women would buy a reformulated Nat Habit scrub on ingredient-trust alone, and existing users already out-rate every other brand on satisfaction. What's missing is a shelf-stable format and a promise as sharp as the category leader's — not more proof that the idea works.

Overview

Why Nat Habit is exploring a new face scrub range, and what this report is built from.

ℹ️Every number on this tab is the whole, unfiltered sample (all 60 survey respondents) — there's no segment lens here on purpose, so Overview always stays a fast, single read. Segment by NH relationship, age, skin type, city tier and more starting on the next tab, Who We Talked To — that filter (picked on the left there) carries through What She Wants and Current Brand & Price too.
About this report — two separate studies of two separate groups of people. Nat Habit's current face scrub, Mura, has a ~2-month shelf life and needs refrigeration — a format that is hard to manufacture and ship, and (per the existing-user research below) suppresses the habit it's meant to build. This report combines three independent sources, kept deliberately apart throughout — every chart, table and KPI is always labelled with which one it's from, and none of the numbers below blend the two respondent groups together: a 60-respondent pre-launch consumer survey (mixed Nat Habit users and non-users, on face scrub attitudes and needs for a NEW range), a separate 50-respondent cohort study of existing Mura users (Active Loyalists, Active Trialists, Active Users, Lapsers and Loyal Lapsers — on real usage of the CURRENT product), and a market landscaping study of 75 competing face-scrub ASINs (third-party category data, not people). Use the Data source bar at the top of the page to view the survey on its own, the cohort study on its own, or both with each section still clearly marked.
Bottom line

The barrier isn't belief, ingredients, or price — it's format and framing.

Nat Habit already wins on the things that are hardest to build: trust (73% of respondents already have some NH relationship) and satisfaction (8.67/10 vs 7.95/10 for every other brand respondents currently use). What it doesn't have is a format that survives daily use without a fridge, or a promise as specific as the category leader's — Niconi captured 60.3% of category revenue from one SKU by fusing an instant tan-removal promise with packaging that signals treatment, not commodity. See the Case for a New Range for the full argument and a scored path forward.

Ingredient deep-dive — named ingredients, grouped into families

What she says would make a scrub more appealing, with every named ingredient grouped into a family (coffee, rice, dal/pulses, spices, butters, fruit & veg, and so on) instead of one vague “natural” bucket — then the same families cross-tabbed against the type of brand she currently uses, to see whether ingredient preference tracks brand choice.

Adjacent categories: face wash & moisturiser

The same "is Nat Habit already winning satisfaction?" question, asked of the two categories she shops right next to face scrub — plus whether she sticks with one brand across all three, or mixes and matches.

Brand-switching patterns — from what type, to what type

Of respondents who named both a previous and a current brand, which kind of brand they left and which kind they landed on — the movement between brand types, not just the reasons given for it.
